exercises.name: intro1
exercises.hint: No hints this time ;)
exercises.description:
This exercise introduces a simple Hello World module in Move for the Sui blockchain.
Your task is to ensure the module compiles successfully.

exercises.name: variables1
exercises.hint: No hint this time
exercises.description:
This exercise requires the module to compile successfully.
Fix the syntax error in the function.

exercises.name: module1
exercises.hint: Add the `public` keyword before `fun`
exercises.description:
A Move module must be declared with `module <address>::<name> { … }`.
In Move, functions are private by default. To call them from other modules,
they must be marked as `public`.

Your task:
Make the `greet` function public so the test module can call it.

When the file compiles **and** the test passes you are done.

exercises.name: module2
exercises.description:
Move lets you `use` a function from another module.
The runner-crate contains a tiny helper module that we can import.

Your task:
1. Add a `use` statement to import `math::add`.
2. Implement `sum_three` using the imported `add` function.

The helper module is automatically available because the
runner-crate’s Move.toml publishes it at address `suilings`.

exercises.name: module3
exercises.hint:
Import vector with: use std::vector;
Then use vector::empty(), vector::push_back()
exercises.description:
In Move, you can use functions and types from other modules by importing them.
The `use` statement allows you to bring items into scope.

Your task:
1. Import the `vector` module from the standard library
2. Use it to create and return a vector with the numbers 1, 2, 3

exercises.name: primitives1
exercises.hint:
u8 holds 0-255, u64 holds much larger numbers.
For add_numbers, use: a + b
exercises.description:
Move has several integer types: u8, u16, u32, u64, u128, u256
Each type has a specific range of values it can hold.

Your task:
Fix the type annotations to make the code compile.

exercises.name: primitives2
exercises.hint:
Use comparison operators: >=, <=, &&
Example: age >= 18 && is_citizen
exercises.description:
Booleans in Move are represented by the `bool` type.
Common operations: && (and), || (or), ! (not), == (equal), != (not equal)

Your task:
Implement the boolean logic functions below.

exercises.name: structs1
exercises.description:
Structs allow you to create custom data types with named fields.
Syntax: struct Name { field1: Type1, field2: Type2 }

Your task:
1. Complete the Person struct with age and name fields
2. Implement the create_person function to instantiate the struct

exercises.name: structs2
exercises.hint:
Abilities are added after struct name: struct Name has copy, drop { ... }
- drop: can be destroyed
- copy: can be copied
- store: can be stored in other structs
exercises.description:
Structs in Move can have abilities: copy, drop, store, and key
- copy: The value can be copied
- drop: The value can be dropped/destroyed
- store: The value can be stored inside other structs
- key: The value can be used as a key for global storage

Your task:
Add the correct abilities to each struct based on the requirements

exercises.name: structs3
exercises.description:
Structs can contain other structs as fields.
This allows you to build complex data structures.

Your task:
Complete the nested struct definitions and implement the functions

exercises.name: structs4
exercises.hint:
Use & for read-only: account.balance
Use &mut for modification: account.balance = new_value
Access fields through reference: account.field_name
exercises.description:
In Move, you can pass structs by reference (&) or mutable reference (&mut).
- & allows reading but not modifying
- &mut allows both reading and modifying

Your task:
Implement functions that work with struct references

exercises.name: structs5
exercises.description:
Generics allow you to write structs that work with any type.
Syntax: struct Name<T> { field: T }
You can also constrain generics with abilities: <T: copy + drop>

Your task:
Complete the generic struct definitions and implement the functions

exercises.name: functions1
exercises.hint:
multiply: return a * b
square: return num * num
max: use if (a > b) a else b
exercises.description:
Functions in Move are declared with the `fun` keyword.
They can have parameters and return values.

Your task:
Implement the functions below following their specifications.

exercises.name: functions2
functions3
exercises.description:
Functions can take mutable references (&mut) to modify values in place.
This is more efficient than copying large values.

Your task:
Implement functions that use mutable references

exercises.name: functions4
exercises.hint:
Generic function: fun name<T: drop>(value: T): T
Type constraints: <T: copy + drop>
Identity: just return value unchanged
exercises.description:
Generic functions work with any type that satisfies the specified constraints.
Syntax: fun name<T: ability>(param: T): T { ... }

Your task:
Implement generic functions that work with multiple types

exercises.name: functions5
exercises.description:
This exercise combines multiple concepts: generics, references, and complex logic.

Your task:
Implement advanced function patterns

exercises.name: control_flow1
exercises.description:
Control flow in Move uses if/else expressions.
Unlike statements, expressions return values!

Your task:
Implement functions using if/else control flow.

exercises.name: control_flow2
exercises.description:
Move supports while loops and loop with break/continue.

while (condition) { ... }
loop { ... break; ... }
continue - skip to next iteration
break - exit the loop

Your task:
Implement functions using loops.

exercises.name: vectors1
exercises.hint:
create_range: Use while loop with vector::push_back
sum_vector: Use while loop with vector::borrow to access elements
reverse_vector: Iterate backwards or pop from original and build new
filter_even: Check num % 2 == 0 before adding to result
exercises.description:
Vectors are growable arrays in Move.

Common operations:
- vector::empty<T>() - create empty vector
- vector::push_back(&mut v, item) - add to end
- vector::pop_back(&mut v) - remove from end
- vector::length(&v) - get size
- vector::borrow(&v, index) - get reference to element
- vector::borrow_mut(&mut v, index) - get mutable reference

Your task:
Implement basic vector operations.

exercises.name: vectors2
exercises.hint:
remove_duplicates: Use vector::contains to check if already added
find_max: Track max value while iterating
merge_sorted: Use two indices, compare elements, add smaller one
chunk_vector: Use nested loop or calculate positions
exercises.description:
More complex vector manipulations and algorithms.

Additional operations:
- vector::contains(&v, &item) - check if item exists
- vector::index_of(&v, &item) - find position
- vector::remove(&mut v, index) - remove at index
- vector::swap(&mut v, i, j) - swap elements

Your task:
Implement advanced vector algorithms.

exercises.name: options1
exercises.hint:
divide: if (b != 0) option::some(a / b) else option::none()
get_or_default: if (option::is_some(&opt)) *option::borrow(&opt) else default
find_in_vector: Use loop to search, return option::some(index) when found
max_of_options: Check both with is_some, compare values if both exist
exercises.description:
Option<T> represents a value that may or may not exist.
It's Move's way of handling nullable values safely.

Option has two variants:
- option::some(value) - contains a value
- option::none() - empty/null

Common operations:
- option::is_some(&opt) - check if has value
- option::is_none(&opt) - check if empty
- option::borrow(&opt) - get reference (panics if none)
- option::contains(&opt, &val) - check specific value
- option::destroy_some(opt) - extract value (panics if none)
- option::destroy_none(opt) - destroy if none (panics if some)

Your task:
Work with Option types to handle optional values.

exercises.name: options2
exercises.description:
Move uses abort and assert for error handling.

- assert!(condition, error_code) - abort if condition is false
- abort error_code - immediately stop execution

Error codes are u64 values that indicate what went wrong.
Best practice: Define error constants with descriptive names.

Your task:
Implement functions with proper error handling.

exercises.name: enums1
exercises.description:
Enums in Move allow you to define a type that can be one of several variants.
Syntax: public enum EnumName { Variant1, Variant2, Variant3 }

Enums are useful for representing states, options, or categories.

Your task:
Create and use basic enums.

exercises.name: enums2
exercises.description:
Match expressions allow you to pattern match on enum variants.
Syntax: match (enum_value) { Variant1 => result1, Variant2 => result2 }

Match is exhaustive - you must handle all variants!

Your task:
Use match expressions to handle enum variants.

exercises.name: enums3
exercises.description:
Enums can have associated data (like Rust's enum variants with data).
Syntax: public enum EnumName { Variant1(Type1), Variant2(Type2) }

When matching, you destructure the data: Variant1(value) => ...

Your task:
Work with enums that contain data.

exercises.name: enums4
exercises.description:
Advanced enum patterns: nested matching, enum methods, and complex data.

Your task:
Implement complex enum operations with nested data structures.

exercises.name: objects1
exercises.description:
In Sui, objects are the fundamental unit of storage.
Objects have unique IDs and can be owned by addresses or shared.

Key abilities for Sui objects:
- key: can be used as a key in global storage (required for objects)
- store: can be stored inside other structs

UID is a unique identifier for objects.
Use object::new(ctx) to create a new UID.

Your task:
Create basic Sui objects with proper abilities.

exercises.name: objects2
exercises.hint:
mint_nft: Create NFT, then use transfer::transfer(nft, sender)
transfer_nft: Just call transfer::transfer(nft, recipient)
create_shared_counter: Create Counter, then transfer::share_object(counter)
increment_counter: counter.value = counter.value + 1
freeze_card: transfer::freeze_object(card)
exercises.description:
Sui objects can be transferred between addresses.

Transfer functions:
- transfer::transfer(obj, recipient) - transfer owned object
- transfer::share_object(obj) - make object shared (anyone can use)
- transfer::freeze_object(obj) - make object immutable

TxContext functions:
- tx_context::sender(ctx) - get the transaction sender

Your task:
Implement object transfers and ownership changes.

exercises.name: events1
exercises.hint:
Event structs need: has copy, drop abilities
TransferEvent: struct TransferEvent has copy, drop { from: address, to: address, amount: u64 }
Emit events: event::emit(TransferEvent { from, to, amount })
Use object::uid_to_inner(&id) to get ID for events
exercises.description:
Events allow smart contracts to emit notifications about state changes.
Events are structs with the 'copy' and 'drop' abilities.

To emit an event:
- event::emit(event_struct)

Events can be queried off-chain to track contract activity.

Your task:
Define and emit events for various contract actions.

exercises.name: strings1
exercises.hint:
Create string: string::utf8(b"text")
Greeting: let mut greeting = string::utf8(b"Hello, "); string::append(&mut greeting, name); string::append(&mut greeting, string::utf8(b"!")); greeting
Length: string::length(&s)
Empty check: string::is_empty(&s)
Concatenate: string::append(&mut s1, s2); s1
Repeat: Use a loop with string::append
exercises.description:
Strings in Move come in two flavors: ASCII and UTF-8.

Common operations:
- string::utf8(bytes) - create UTF-8 string from bytes
- ascii::string(bytes) - create ASCII string from bytes
- string::length(s) - get length
- string::is_empty(s) - check if empty
- string::append(s1, s2) - concatenate strings
- string::as_bytes(s) - get underlying bytes

Your task:
Implement basic string operations using Move's string module.

exercises.name: strings2
exercises.hint:
Substring: string::sub_string(&s, start, end)
Contains: option::is_some(&string::index_of(&haystack, &needle))
Starts with: Check length first, then compare substring(s, 0, prefix_len) == prefix
Ends with: substring(s, s_len - suffix_len, s_len) == suffix
Count char: let bytes = string::bytes(&s); loop through vector, count matches
Uppercase: Loop through bytes, if byte >= 97 && byte <= 122, subtract 32
exercises.description:
Advanced string operations in Move.

String manipulation:
- string::substring(s, start, end) - extract substring
- string::index_of(s, substring) - find index of substring
- Working with bytes for character operations

Your task:
Implement advanced string operations.

exercises.name: storage1
exercises.hint:
Store objects: Objects with 'store' ability can be stored in vectors inside other objects
Add to vector: vector::push_back(&mut parent.children, child)
Count: vector::length(&parent.children)
exercises.description:
Storage in Sui: Objects with 'store' ability can be stored inside other objects.
Objects stored in other objects become part of the parent object.

Your task:
Learn to store objects inside other objects using the 'store' ability.

exercises.name: storage2
exercises.hint:
Remove from vector: vector::remove(&mut container.items, index) returns the item
Add to vector: vector::push_back(&mut container.items, item)
Count: vector::length(&container.items)
exercises.description:
Advanced storage operations: removing children and working with multiple children.

Your task:
Implement functions to remove children from storage and manage collections.

exercises.name: storage3
exercises.hint:
Key-value storage: Use parallel vectors for keys and values
Add: vector::push_back for both keys and values vectors
Count: vector::length (should be same for both vectors)
exercises.description:
Storage with maps: storing and retrieving values by key using vectors.

In Move, we can simulate key-value storage using vectors and helper functions.

Your task:
Work with key-value storage patterns for flexible data storage.

exercises.name: ownership1
exercises.description:
Ownership in Move is unique - each value has exactly one owner.
When you pass a value to a function, ownership is transferred (moved).
You cannot use a value after it's been moved!

Your task:
Understand basic ownership transfer.

exercises.name: ownership2
exercises.hint:
Use & for read-only: fun read(counter: &Counter)
Use &mut for modification: fun increment(counter: &mut Counter)
References don't transfer ownership
exercises.description:
References allow you to borrow values without taking ownership.
- &T: immutable reference (read-only)
- &mut T: mutable reference (can modify)

References don't transfer ownership, so the original value can still be used.

Your task:
Use references to avoid transferring ownership.

exercises.name: ownership3
exercises.hint:
Copy ability: struct Point has copy, drop { ... } can be copied
Without copy: values are moved (ownership transferred)
Copy allows: (point, point) - same value used twice
exercises.description:
Copy vs Move: Types with 'copy' ability can be copied instead of moved.
Without 'copy', values are moved (ownership transferred).

Your task:
Understand when values are copied vs moved.

exercises.name: ownership4
exercises.hint:
Nested structs: account.wallet.balance
Extract from nested: let Account { wallet, transactions: _ } = account; wallet
Modify through reference: account.wallet.balance = new_value
exercises.description:
Advanced ownership: nested structures, borrowing fields, and ownership in collections.

Your task:
Handle ownership with complex data structures.

exercises.name: uid_id1
exercises.hint:
Get ID from object: object::id(&obj)
Convert UID to ID: object::uid_to_inner(&uid)
Compare IDs: id1 == id2
exercises.description:
UID (Unique Identifier) and ID are fundamental types in Sui.
- UID: Internal unique identifier for objects (used in struct definitions)
- ID: Public identifier that can be used to reference objects
- object::id(obj) converts UID to ID
- object::uid_to_inner(&uid) converts UID to ID

Your task:
Learn to work with UID and ID types.

exercises.name: uid_id2
exercises.hint:
Store IDs: vector::push_back(&mut ids, object::id(&token))
Check ID: Loop through vector and compare IDs
Count: vector::length(&ids)
exercises.description:
Working with UID and ID in object relationships.
Objects can reference other objects by ID.

Your task:
Store and retrieve object IDs in relationships.

exercises.name: uid_id3
exercises.hint:
Get ID: object::id(&asset) or object::uid_to_inner(&asset.id)
Use in events: event::emit(Event { asset_id: object::id(&asset), ... })
ID is copyable and can be stored in events
exercises.description:
Advanced UID/ID operations: converting between types and using in events.

Your task:
Use UID and ID in various contexts including events and object references.

exercises.name: receiving1
exercises.hint:
Entry function: public entry fun receive(obj: ObjectType, ctx: &mut TxContext)
Transfer: transfer::transfer(obj, recipient)
Destroy: Let object go out of scope or destructure it
exercises.description:
Receiving objects in Sui entry functions.
Entry functions can receive objects as parameters.
Objects passed to entry functions are consumed (moved).

Syntax: public entry fun function_name(obj: ObjectType, ctx: &mut TxContext)

Your task:
Create entry functions that receive and process objects.

exercises.name: receiving2
exercises.hint:
Multiple objects: public entry fun func(obj1: Type1, obj2: Type2, ctx: &mut TxContext)
Transfer multiple: transfer::transfer for each object
Combine values: Extract values, create new object, transfer it
exercises.description:
Receiving multiple objects and processing them together.
Entry functions can receive multiple objects as parameters.

Your task:
Handle multiple objects in entry functions.

exercises.name: receiving3
exercises.hint:
Mutable shared objects: public entry fun func(obj: &mut SharedObject)
Modify: obj.field = new_value
Combine operations: Modify object, then transfer or destroy other objects
exercises.description:
Advanced receiving patterns: shared objects and object mutations.
Entry functions can receive and modify shared objects.

Your task:
Handle shared objects and mutable operations in entry functions.

exercises.name: generics1
exercises.description:
Generics in Move can have multiple type parameters and constraints.

Phantom type parameters are used when a type parameter doesn't appear
in any fields but is needed for type safety.

Multiple constraints: <T: copy + drop + store>

Your task:
Work with advanced generic patterns.

exercises.name: generics2
exercises.hint:
Stack: struct Stack<T: drop> has drop { items: vector<T> }
Push: vector::push_back(&mut stack.items, item)
Pop: vector::pop_back(&mut stack.items)
Peek: vector::borrow(&stack.items, vector::length(&stack.items) - 1)
Queue: struct Queue<T: drop> has drop { items: vector<T> }
Enqueue: vector::push_back(&mut queue.items, item)
Dequeue: vector::remove(&mut queue.items, 0)
exercises.description:
Generic container types in Move.

You can build reusable container types using generics.
Common patterns include Stack, Queue, and Wrapper types.

Type constraints ensure elements have required abilities:
- store: can be stored in global storage
- copy: can be copied
- drop: can be dropped/discarded

Your task:
Implement a generic Stack and Queue.

exercises.name: generics3
exercises.description:
Advanced generic patterns: Phantom types and type constraints.

Phantom types are type parameters that don't appear in struct fields
but are used for type-level programming and compile-time safety.

Example use cases:
- Type-safe state machines
- Currency types without runtime overhead
- Capability patterns

Your task:
Implement type-safe wrappers using phantom types.
